details.expected: Driving begins with a choice: whether this person, this vehicle and this journey are ready to go together. Sweden’s Vision Zero (Nollvisionen) aims for no one to be killed or seriously injured in traffic. The choices taught here contribute to that aim. details.expected: Requirements. For an ordinary new category B licence, you need a valid learner permit, permanent residence in Sweden or at least six months of study here, the minimum age of 18, valid car risk training, and successful theory and practical tests. Holding another EEA licence affects the application route. Category B normally covers a passenger car or light goods vehicle with a registered maximum weight of no more than 3,500 kg; trailers are explained in module 8. Check any conditions on your entitlement, including an automatic-transmission restriction. Transportstyrelsen: category B

details.expected: Private practice requires an approved supervisor for the particular learner. The learner normally needs a group 1 permit. Practice in a passenger car can begin at 16; the minimum is 17 years and 6 months for practice with a light goods vehicle or a light trailer. The supervisor is legally treated as the driver, must carry proof of approval, and the practice sign must be clearly visible from behind. Exceptions concerning an existing entitlement must be checked against your own circumstances. Transportstyrelsen: category B

Sleep and safe judgement

details.expected: Medical explanation · Sleep and awareness. Microsleep (mikrosömn) is a brief, unintended episode of sleep. You do not choose it or reliably prevent it by deciding to try harder. For a deliberately hypothetical two-second lapse at a constant 90 km/h, distance = speed × time: 90 ÷ 3.6 = 25 metres per second; 25 × 2 = 50 metres travelled while asleep. Two seconds is an example, not a prediction of how long a microsleep lasts. CDC/NIOSH: microsleeps

Two seconds is an example, not a prediction of how long a microsleep lasts. CDC/NIOSH: microsleeps

details.expected: Official safety advice · Replace missing sleep with sleep. Adequate sleep is the fundamental remedy for sleep deprivation. Coffee or an energy drink may briefly make you feel more alert, but does not replace the sleep you need; serious sleep deprivation can still lead to microsleep. Music, an open window or willpower should not be treated as a clearance to drive: they do not provide the missing sleep. Do not start when you cannot stay awake; if sleepiness develops, stop somewhere safe and arrange rest or another way to travel. See M07-L03 for planning around fatigue on a journey. NHTSA: drowsy driving

details.expected: Medical explanation · Stimulation is not safe judgement. Stimulant misuse, for example involving amphetamine or cocaine, can produce overconfidence while judgement and concentration are impaired. Some stimulant effects can reduce the feeling of fatigue or drowsiness: tiredness may be masked rather than the need for sleep removed. Feeling energetic is therefore not proof of safe driving ability. Effects vary with substance, dose and individual circumstances; this does not mean every prescribed stimulant treatment has the same effect. Ask your prescriber about your treatment and driving. Swedish Government: stimulant confidence and judgement · NHTSA: stimulant effects

details.expected: Official policy aim · Vision Zero. Nollvisionen means no one should be killed or seriously injured in traffic. It is not a promise that nobody will ever make a mistake. Trafikverket describes shared responsibility: road users must show consideration and judgement and follow traffic rules, while system designers have ultimate responsibility for the system’s safety. Your part includes choosing safe speed and margins and refusing a pressured manoeuvre; road and vehicle design also contribute. For example, staying behind a vehicle near a hidden crest helps protect people even when a passenger dislikes the delay. Trafikverket: Vision Zero

details.expected: ABS in an emergency. Anti-lock braking helps prevent wheel locking and can preserve steering control. details.expected: Technical explanation · Head restraints. In a rear impact, the seat and torso can move while the head lags behind. A correctly designed and adjusted head restraint helps limit damaging head movement relative to the torso and reduce neck-injury risk. Trafikverket advises positioning the top at the crown of the head and keeping the gap behind the head as small as possible. Adjust it for the occupant before driving; a comfort setting is not the same as a protective setting. A head restraint cannot guarantee that injury will be avoided. Trafikverket: seats and head restraints

details.expected: Why children face backwards. A young child's head is relatively heavy and the neck is vulnerable. In a frontal collision, a rear-facing seat supports the head and body together, takes up collision forces and distributes the load across the supported body. The neck does not have to restrain the heavy head on its own in the same way as when facing forwards. This is why the recommendations above concern protection, not only seat orientation. Follow the seat's size limits, fitting instructions and airbag compatibility. Trafikverket: child head and neck protection · Transportstyrelsen: rear-facing collision protection
details.observed: Why children face backwards. A young child's head is relatively heavy and the neck is vulnerable. In a frontal collision, a rear-facing seat supports the head and body together, takes up collision forces and distributes the load across the supported body. The neck does not have to restrain the heavy head on its own in the same way as when facing forwards. This is why the recommendations above concern protection, not only seat orientation. Follow the seat's size limits, fitting instructions and airbag compatibility. Trafikverket: child head and neck protection · Transportstyrelsen: rear-facing collision protection

details.expected: Think of stopping in two parts. During the time between noticing a hazard and beginning effective braking, the vehicle still travels. After that, it travels while slowing. details.expected: Safety advice · Check a timed gap. For the three-second following-distance guideline, select a fixed roadside point, such as a pole or sign. When the rear of the vehicle ahead passes it, start counting at a steady seconds pace. Stop when the front of your car reaches the same point. Arriving before three seconds indicates a short gap against that guideline: ease back smoothly and check again. Three seconds is a guideline, not a statutory fixed interval or a guarantee; poor grip, visibility or other hazards require more space and an appropriate speed. Keep observing the road while counting. NSW Government: fixed-point following-gap method

details.expected: Fixed-point example. The car ahead passes a sign. You count “one thousand and one, one thousand and two, one thousand and three”. A timed gap therefore represents more metres at higher speed, without requiring you to estimate metres by eye.

details.expected: Physical explanation · Twice the speed. With the same effective grip and braking deceleration on the same gradient, braking distance is approximately proportional to speed squared: 2 × speed → 4 × braking distance. In a constant-deceleration model, distance = speed² ÷ (2 × deceleration), with speed in metres per second. Doubling speed multiplies the numerator by four. Real conditions and brake response can change; this is a comparison under stated assumptions. Trafikverket: VGU braking-distance equation

details.expected: Hypothetical comparison. Assume a level road, unchanged vehicle/load/grip, constant braking deceleration of 5 m/s² and a one-second response delay. At 40 km/h, braking distance is about 12.3 m and reaction distance 11.1 m. At 80 km/h they are 49.4 m and 22.2 m: braking quadruples while reaction distance doubles. Total stopping distances are about 23.5 m and 71.6 m, so the total does not quadruple. These invented model conditions explain the relationship; they are not predicted stopping distances for your car.

details.expected: Knowledge check. (1) If response delay doubles at the same speed, what happens to reaction distance? (2) How do you time a three-second following gap? (3) Why increase the forward gap when someone follows too closely? (4) With unchanged braking deceleration, how does doubled speed affect braking distance, and does total stopping distance also quadruple? (5) Complete the three approximate exercises above and explain why you should keep exact reaction conversion separate. Answer: (1) It doubles under the constant-speed assumption. (2) Count seconds from the rear of the car ahead passing a fixed point until your front reaches that point; three seconds is a guideline and conditions may require more. (3) More forward space allows gentler slowing and gives the follower more time; avoid unnecessary sudden braking. (4) Braking distance becomes approximately four times as long, but reaction distance doubles for the same response delay, so the combined total does not generally quadruple. (5) A: reaction 4.5 m, braking 3.6 m, total 8.1 m. B: reaction 24 m, braking 25.6 m, total 49.6 m. C: reaction 60 m, braking 40 m, total 100 m. Use both rough equations together; substituting exact reaction conversion changes the exercise-model answer.

details.expected: Knowledge check. (1) Does a narrow visible gap beside a cyclist prove passing is safe? (2) A bus signals from its stop on a 70 km/h road while you drive at 40. Does the special bus rule apply, and what must both drivers do? (3) Should you greet a working guide dog? (4) Is a person riding a pedal bicycle operating a vehicle? Answer: (1) No. Consider possible rider movement, obstacles, oncoming traffic and a safe lateral margin; wait if needed. (2) No: the road limit determines the threshold. The bus must enter safely without unnecessary obstruction; you must adapt speed to facilitate the observed entry into your lane. At limits of 50 or lower, slow and let the bus leave, stopping if necessary; the bus driver must take particular care. details.expected: Restrictions to recognise. Overtaking is generally prohibited immediately before or in a road junction, with specified exceptions for right-side overtaking, police/signal control, or an established yielding/stopping duty on the crossing road. Similar restrictions apply at level crossings, with exceptions for barriers or road-junction-type traffic signals. At an obscured bend or crest, do not use an opposing lane to overtake; the detailed provision contains limited exceptions. Section 39 also contains an exception for passing two-wheeled vehicles without sidecars. That exception does not override the danger prohibition, continuous-line restrictions or the uncontrolled-crossing prohibition. None of these exceptions proves a manoeuvre safe. details.expected: Requirements. Your speed must allow a stop within the visible road and before foreseeable hazards. details.expected: Use main beam when needed for a sufficient field of view, but not where the road is adequately lit, where it can dazzle an approaching driver or an adjacent rail/ship operator, or at close distance behind another vehicle. Dipped beam is the usual driving light. In fog or heavy precipitation, front fog lights may replace dipped beam; the prohibited combinations must not be used together. A rear fog light is restricted to fog, heavy precipitation or comparable reduced visibility and must not dazzle a following driver. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§69–72

details.expected: Peripheral vision · Notice, then inspect. Peripheral or side vision surrounds your direct focus. It can alert you to movement, a developing hazard or a traffic change outside that focus. Move your eyes, and head where needed, to inspect the relevant object directly while maintaining control and awareness of the road. For example, notice movement near the verge, then look to identify whether it is a person about to enter your path. Keep scanning; staring at one sign can leave other information unattended. Official driver-vision guidance

details.expected: Tyres need friction to change the vehicle's speed and direction. Braking while cornering shares that capacity; ABS can help preserve steering forces during braking, but the available friction still limits the result. Water, snow and ice change the conditions at the tyre contact, so dry-road expectations cannot simply be carried into them. VTI friction report, sections 4.2–4.3

details.expected: Requirements for ordinary light cars and their trailers, checked 1 October 2026. Between 1 December and 31 March, winter tyres or equivalent equipment are required when winter conditions exist. Snow, ice, slush or frost on any part of the road counts; police determine conditions at the location. The minimum tread depth for the ordinary light-vehicle case is 3 mm. Studless winter tyres for the car need the mountain/snowflake marking. Winter tyres

details.expected: Studded tyres are permitted from 1 October to 15 April and outside that period when winter conditions exist or are expected. Do not mix studded and non-studded tyres on an ordinary passenger car or light goods vehicle. In winter conditions, a studded towing car requires a studded trailer; the reverse combination is allowed. A light-trailer transition permits specified winter-designed M+S tyres through 30 November 2028. Exemptions and heavier-vehicle cases need their own checks; they are not the ordinary car rule. Winter tyres · Traffic Regulation, chapter 4 §§18a–18d

details.expected: Surface change · A bridge can freeze first. A bridge is exposed to cold air above and below. That exposure can cool it faster than neighbouring road supported by ground, so moisture can freeze on the bridge while the approach still appears clear. It is a possibility, not a rule that every bridge always freezes first. Anticipate uncertain grip and reduce speed before reaching the bridge. National Weather Service: bridge cooling

details.expected: Rain on a cold road · Ice can hide. Rainwater can freeze when it meets a road surface cold enough for ice to form, producing a thin, nearly invisible slippery layer. The road may look wet, and the air temperature can be above zero while the surface is still below freezing. Near-zero air alone does not prove ice, but it calls for attention to surface conditions, more space and lower speed. Trafikverket: deceptive ice and cold roads

details.expected: First rain after dry weather · Residues matter. During a dry spell, dust, dirt and oily residues can accumulate. The first rain can mix with these contaminants and make the road unusually slippery. Reassess speed and separation as rain starts; do not assume a light shower immediately washes the surface clean or that a fixed time restores grip. County Fire: rain after a dry spell

details.expected: Rear stability · Why the best grip belongs at the rear. Transportstyrelsen recommends the best-grip or deepest-tread tyres at the rear to reduce skid risk in braking and bends, for both front- and rear-wheel-drive cars. Better rear grip helps reduce the risk of the rear sliding outward and rotating the car. Suitable tyres and stability assistance still cannot guarantee control. Transportstyrelsen: best tyres at the rear · VTI: rear grip and oversteer

details.expected: Oversteer · Rear grip loss. In the loss-of-grip situation, the rear tyres lose sufficient lateral grip, the tail swings outward and the car rotates more than intended into the turn. This can develop into a spin. VTI: oversteer and rear stability

details.expected: Understeer · Front grip loss. In the loss-of-grip situation, the front tyres cannot supply the lateral grip needed for the requested turn. The car turns less than intended and follows a straighter, wider path; adding more steering does not guarantee the requested curve. These are grip-loss explanations, not a full definition of every vehicle's normal handling characteristics. VTI: handling paths · NHTSA: front-axle grip limit

details.expected: Aquaplaning · Water interrupts contact. If water builds between tyres and road, it can support the tyre on a film and reduce or remove effective tyre-road contact. Steering and braking then have less grip to work with. Reduce speed before standing water and uncertain wet surfaces. PennDOT: aquaplaning

details.expected: Response · Ease off smoothly. If aquaplaning starts and there is space to slow gradually, ease off the accelerator, keep steering steady and avoid abrupt steering or hard braking. Make only gentle necessary corrections as contact returns. This is different from M02-L01's ABS emergency-stop instruction: ABS cannot create grip where a tyre is separated from the road by water. An immediate collision emergency needs action appropriate to the actual situation; this advice does not establish a universal ban on braking. PennDOT: aquaplaning response

details.expected: Requirements. Municipalities can introduce environmental zones under the national framework. Class 1 concerns heavy buses and heavy goods vehicles; class 2 concerns passenger cars and light buses/goods vehicles. If a breakdown leaves a vehicle where stopping is prohibited, it must be moved to a suitable place as soon as possible, subject to the special rules for an accident scene. Warning obligations depend on the situation. A warning triangle must give approaching drivers enough warning; the law does not prescribe one universal distance for every road. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§51 and 57

details.expected: Official motorway/2+1-road advice. If possible, reach the safest available stopping place. Switch on hazard lights, warn other traffic and leave the vehicle and carriageway promptly. Move away from traffic, outside a barrier where one exists. Trafikverket recommends placing the triangle at least 100 m away, preferably farther, and taking care while doing so, walking at the side and outside the barrier where possible. Do not expose yourself in the traffic lane to carry out a roadside repair. Call professional recovery; call 112 when life is in danger. Trafikverket: breakdown advice

details.expected: Tunnel advice is different. Use hazard lights, move towards the edge or an emergency bay if possible and switch off the engine. For a non-urgent incident, Trafikverket advises staying in the car or protected from traffic close to it while calling for assistance. In an urgent situation, leave for the nearest emergency exit and use the assistance point, emergency phone or 112. In a fire, leave and reach an emergency exit; follow signs, announcements and emergency personnel. Do not turn a non-urgent-tunnel recommendation into advice to stay beside a fire. Trafikverket: tunnels

details.expected: Overheating · Leave the hot cap closed. In a conventional pressurised cooling system, hot coolant and steam can remain under pressure even after the engine is switched off. Opening the radiator cap, or the cap of a pressurised coolant reservoir, can release that pressure and expel scalding liquid or steam, causing severe burns. Never loosen or remove the cap while the engine or cooling system is hot. Switching off is not proof that pressure and heat have disappeared. Manufacturer handbook: hot coolant and pressure warning

details.expected: Apply the warning. The temperature warning appears on a motorway journey. After reaching the safest available stopping place as conditions allow, follow the vehicle's stopping instructions and this lesson's motorway scene-safety advice. A passenger suggests opening the coolant cap immediately because the engine is now off. Reject that action: residual heat and pressure can still cause a burn. Call recovery from a protected position rather than attempting an exposed repair. If the event is in a tunnel, use the tunnel response above; smoke, fire or danger to life requires the urgent response, not waiting beside the vehicle to diagnose it. Trafikverket: motorway breakdown · Trafikverket: tunnel urgency

details.expected: Wildlife collisions. Trafikverket advises calling 112 and marking the collision location safely so responders can find it, even if the animal has left. Avoid approaching an injured animal. Its guidance gives a separate precaution for wild boar, bear, lynx and wolf: continue 200 m before stopping and marking, then call police immediately. Only move the vehicle when safe and possible; explain the actual collision location and the animal's direction clearly. This is agency safety guidance, not a claim that every animal species has identical statutory reporting rules. Trafikverket: wildlife collisions

details.expected: Study group What to practise Related lessons Warning signs (A) Identify the hazard and choose an earlier observation or speed response. M03-L01, M06-L01, M07 Priority signs (B) State whether to stop or yield and identify the conflicting traffic. M04-L01/L03/L04 Prohibitions (C) Determine the restricted action, vehicle, weight, dimension or speed and its extent. M03-L01, M05-L03, M08 Mandatory and instruction signs (D/E) Choose the required path or recognise a road/area regime and its end. M03, M05-L02, M06-L03 Directions, including walking/cycling directions (F) Identify the destination and mode, choose a lane early and avoid a late turn. M03-L03 Public facilities, services and tourism (G/H/I) Locate a destination while still checking access rules. M03-L03 Information and symbols (J/S) Read the actual message and the road-user or facility symbol. M03-L02/L03 Supplementary panels (T) Combine the main sign with time, distance, length, direction or vehicle qualifications. M03-L02, M05-L03 Markings (M) Distinguish lane boundaries, warnings, crossing locations and stopping/parking instructions. M03-L02, M04, M05-L03 Signals (SIG) Identify which traffic is controlled and what the current indication requires. M03-L02, M04-L03 Police and guard instructions (P/V) Recognise an authorised direction and respond to it.
